subtitle: The passive with a modal, and in the Perfekt
words.intro: Berlin’s new airport was due to open in 2011. It opened in 2020. For nine years, trains ran empty to its station to keep the air fresh, and German gained a sentence: *Das muss noch geprüft werden.*

grammar[0].fact: German has a word for a cost-and-time disaster of this size: *ein Großprojekt*. Hamburg’s concert hall, Stuttgart’s station and Berlin’s airport are the big three. Germans who pride themselves on engineering are not quite sure how to talk about them.

grammar[1].blocks[1].blocks[0].title: worden or geworden?
grammar[1].blocks[1].blocks[0].text: *Das Haus ist gebaut worden* (passive). *Er ist Arzt geworden* (became).
grammar[1].blocks[2].title: Words for the practice page
grammar[1].fact: The rule is simple, and Germans still pause over it: *Er ist Arzt geworden* (he became a doctor), but *Er ist operiert worden* (he was operated on). The *ge-* falls away only in the passive.

document.intro: A real sign at the airport, in German and in English. It’s short: *der Übergang* is the passage. An airport is a good place to pair each German sign with its English twin.
document.fact: When the airport finally opened, in the middle of the pandemic, hardly anyone was flying. The first planes landed in the rain. Its Terminal 2 stood empty for a long time, and the jokes began all over again.
document.tasks[1].instruction: Turn each sentence into the passive, in the Perfekt.
reading.intro: A press conference at a new airport in a German city that would prefer not to be named. The opening has been moved for the seventh time. Max has come along with a journalist friend, and he has a simple question. The spokeswoman, Frau Dr. Stark, has a printed answer for everything.
reading.fact: Berlin Brandenburg Airport began in 2006, was to open in 2011, and in the end opened in October 2020, at several times the original cost. Fire safety was among the main problems. Its empty station was aired by trains for years, and comedians have never been so well fed.
